definition: The information of one outcome, which is larger when that outcome is less probable.
wrongs: The average uncertainty of a whole source.
The number of bits in a fixed-length computer word.
The power of additive noise on a channel.
why: A rare event is more surprising, so its information, minus the log of its probability, is larger.
example: Learning that a fair coin landed heads is one bit; a one-in-a-million lottery win carries far more.
scenario: Event A has probability 1/2 and event B has probability 1/16. Which event carries more self-information?
scenarioWhy: The rarer event has the larger self-information.

definition: The average information of the outcomes of a source, measuring that source's uncertainty.
wrongs: The information of one particular outcome only.
The highest rate of a noisy channel.
The Hamming distance between two codewords.
why: Entropy averages self-information over the source distribution and is the lossless coding limit.
example: A fair coin has entropy of one bit, while a coin that always lands heads has entropy zero.
scenario: A source symbol is certain to be the same value every time. What is that source's entropy?
scenarioWhy: A source with no uncertainty has entropy zero.

definition: The entropy of a binary source that emits one symbol with probability p and the other with probability 1-p.
wrongs: The entropy of any source whose alphabet has more than two symbols.
The capacity of every Gaussian channel.
The length of a Huffman code for English text.
why: It depends only on p, is zero at the extremes, and reaches one bit when p is one half.
example: A biased coin with p equal to 0.1 has binary entropy well below one bit per toss.
scenario: For a coin, binary entropy is largest when the probability of heads equals which value?
scenarioWhy: A fair binary source is the most uncertain, so its entropy peaks at one half.

definition: The uncertainty of a pair of random variables taken together.
wrongs: The uncertainty that remains in one variable after the other is observed.
The information shared by two variables.
The entropy of only the first variable.
why: It is the entropy of the combined outcome, not the leftover uncertainty or the shared part.
example: The joint entropy of two fair independent coin tosses is two bits.
scenario: Two fair coins are independent. How many bits of joint entropy do the two tosses have?
scenarioWhy: Independent fair bits add, so the pair has two bits of joint entropy.

definition: The uncertainty that remains about one random variable after another variable is observed.
wrongs: The uncertainty of both variables before any observation.
The information one variable gives about the other.
The self-information of a single sure event.
why: Conditioning cannot raise uncertainty, and independent side information leaves entropy unchanged.
example: After a noiseless channel output is seen, the conditional entropy of the input is zero.
scenario: Y is an exact copy of X. Once Y is observed, how much uncertainty about X remains?
scenarioWhy: Knowing an exact copy removes all uncertainty, so the conditional entropy is zero.

definition: The amount of information that one random variable reveals about another.
wrongs: The remaining uncertainty of a variable after the other is known.
The joint uncertainty of a pair before any observation.
The energy of the transmitted signal.
why: It equals the drop in uncertainty about one variable when the other is observed, and it is zero if they are independent.
example: A noiseless link has mutual information equal to the input entropy, because the output reveals the input fully.
scenario: X and Y are independent fair bits. How much mutual information do they share?
scenarioWhy: Independent variables reveal nothing about each other, so mutual information is zero.

definition: The information that two variables still share after a third variable is already known.
wrongs: The mutual information of two variables with no side information.
The entropy of the third variable alone.
The Hamming distance of a code.
why: It measures dependence that remains once the known variable's contribution is removed.
example: Given today's weather, yesterday's reading may still say something about tomorrow's reading.
scenario: Z already fixes everything X and Y share, so they are independent once Z is known. Their conditional mutual information is:
scenarioWrongs: The joint entropy of X and Y
scenarioWhy: If nothing remains between X and Y after Z is known, conditional mutual information is zero.

definition: Joint entropy equals the entropy of one variable plus the conditional entropy of the other given the first.
wrongs: Joint entropy equals the product of the two separate entropies.
Conditional entropy is always larger than joint entropy.
Mutual information equals the sum of the two entropies.
why: Uncertainty of a pair splits into uncertainty of the first outcome plus what the second still adds.
example: For two dependent bits, the pair's entropy is the first bit's entropy plus the second bit's entropy given the first.
scenario: H(X) is 1 bit and H(Y|X) is 0.5 bit. What is the joint entropy H(X,Y)?
scenarioWhy: The chain rule adds H(X) and H(Y|X), giving 1.5 bits.

definition: The extra average information cost of using an assumed distribution instead of the true one.
wrongs: A symmetric distance that is always equal in both directions.
The capacity of a binary symmetric channel.
The minimum Hamming distance of a code.
why: It is the expected log ratio of the true probabilities to the assumed ones, and it is not symmetric.
example: Coding a biased coin as if it were fair costs extra bits equal to the divergence from fair to the true bias.
scenario: A code is designed for distribution q while the source really follows p. Which quantity is the extra bit cost?
scenarioWhy: The penalty for assuming the wrong distribution is the KL divergence.

definition: The average bits used when events from a true distribution are coded as if another distribution were true.
wrongs: The entropy of the true source alone, with a matched code.
The mutual information across a noiseless channel.
The number of parity bits in a Hamming code.
why: It equals the true entropy plus the divergence caused by the mismatched code.
example: An English model trained on news uses more bits per character on poetry than the poetry source's own entropy.
scenario: Symbols are drawn from p but encoded with ideal code lengths for a different distribution q. Which average length is that?
scenarioWhy: The average length of a code matched to the wrong distribution is cross-entropy.

definition: The average uncertainty per symbol of a long sequence from a random process.
wrongs: The entropy of one isolated symbol, ignoring dependence on neighbours.
The peak mutual information of a channel.
The raw bit rate of a modem in hertz.
why: For a stationary process it is the limit of the joint entropy of n symbols divided by n.
example: English text has a much lower entropy rate per letter than independent uniform letters would.
scenario: A memoryless source has symbol entropy H. What is its entropy rate per symbol?
scenarioWhy: With no dependence between symbols, the entropy rate equals the single-symbol entropy.

definition: A source that emits independent symbols from a fixed finite alphabet with unchanging probabilities.
wrongs: A source whose next symbol depends on the previous symbol.
A continuous waveform source such as unquantised speech.
A channel that flips bits at random.
why: Each symbol is drawn afresh from the same distribution, so the entropy rate equals one symbol's entropy.
example: Repeated independent tosses of one biased coin form a discrete memoryless source.
scenario: Each symbol is drawn independently from the same three-symbol distribution. Which source model is that?
scenarioWhy: Independent identical draws from a finite alphabet are a discrete memoryless source.

definition: Representing source symbols with bit strings so the average number of bits is reduced.
wrongs: Adding structured parity so a channel decoder can correct errors.
Modulating bits onto a radio carrier.
Encrypting bits so an eavesdropper cannot read them.
why: Source coding exploits uneven probabilities or repetition; it does not protect against channel noise.
example: A compressor assigns short bit strings to frequent letters and longer strings to rare letters.
scenario: A program assigns short bit strings to common letters before any noise protection is added. Which task is that?
scenarioWhy: Compressing the source into fewer bits is source coding.

definition: Lossless coding of a memoryless source can approach its entropy, but cannot average fewer bits than that.
wrongs: Any source can be losslessly coded down to zero bits.
Reliable communication is possible above channel capacity.
Every prefix code must have equal-length codewords.
why: Shannon showed entropy is the greatest lower bound on average length for lossless recovery.
example: A source of entropy 0.5 bit per symbol cannot be losslessly compressed to 0.2 bit per symbol on average.
scenario: A memoryless source has entropy 0.5 bit per symbol. Which average lossless length is impossible?
scenarioWhy: The source coding theorem forbids a lossless average below the entropy.

definition: A method that builds an optimal prefix code by repeatedly merging the two least probable symbols.
wrongs: A universal dictionary method that does not use symbol probabilities in advance.
Repeating each bit three times for majority voting.
A code that intentionally allows one codeword to be a prefix of another.
why: Merging rare symbols first yields a prefix code with the smallest average length for those symbol probabilities.
example: Symbols with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.25 receive Huffman lengths 1, 2, and 2.
scenario: A coder repeatedly combines the two rarest remaining symbols until one tree remains. Which algorithm is that?
scenarioWhy: Merging least probable symbols is the Huffman construction.

definition: A code in which no codeword is a prefix of another codeword, so decoding can stop at each word.
wrongs: A code that needs a separating comma because words can begin other words.
A code whose only goal is correcting channel errors.
A code that uses the same bit string for two different symbols.
why: The decoder recognises a complete word as soon as it arrives, without looking ahead.
example: The set {0, 10, 11} is prefix-free, while {0, 01} is not because 0 begins 01.
scenario: Codewords are 0, 10, and 11. Can the decoder tell when each word ends without lookahead?
scenarioWrongs: Only if a comma is inserted
scenarioWhy: No codeword prefixes another, so the set is instantaneously decodable.

definition: A length test that says whether a binary prefix code with those codeword lengths can exist.
wrongs: A bound on the minimum distance needed to correct errors.
A formula for the entropy of a fair coin only.
A rule that every codeword must have the same length.
why: For binary prefix codes the sum of two to the minus each length must be at most one.
example: Lengths 1, 2, and 2 meet the test because 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 equals 1.
scenario: Proposed binary lengths are 1, 2, 2, and 2. Can they belong to a prefix code?
scenarioWrongs: Only if the source is fair
Only for a Huffman tree of English
scenarioWhy: One half plus three quarters is greater than one, so Kraft's inequality fails.

definition: How far a source's entropy falls below the logarithm of its alphabet size.
wrongs: The parity bits added by a channel code.
The mutual information of a noiseless channel.
The delay spread of a radio path.
why: A uniform source has no redundancy; bias or structure leaves room for compression.
example: A two-symbol source with entropy 0.5 bit has half a bit of redundancy relative to one uncompressed bit.
scenario: A four-symbol source has entropy 1 bit, while equal-length coding would use 2 bits. How much source redundancy is that?
scenarioWhy: Redundancy is log of the alphabet size minus entropy, here 2 minus 1.

definition: Compression that allows the original symbol sequence to be reconstructed exactly.
wrongs: Compression that deliberately discards detail to go below the entropy.
Coding that only detects channel bit flips.
Quantisation that maps many amplitudes to one level.
why: The mapping is reversible, so the average rate cannot beat the source entropy.
example: A zip archive of a text file expands back to the identical bytes.
scenario: A compressed file must expand to the exact original essay, with no missing characters. Which compression class is required?
scenarioWhy: Exact reconstruction requires lossless compression.

definition: Compression that accepts a controlled difference so the rate can fall below the source entropy.
wrongs: Compression that always restores every original bit.
A prefix code that only shortens frequent symbols.
A parity bit that detects a single flip.
why: Discarding imperceptible or tolerable detail removes information on purpose.
example: A lecture recording saved as a low-rate audio file does not match the original samples exactly.
scenario: An image coder throws away detail the eye rarely notices and cannot restore the exact pixels. Which class is that?
scenarioWhy: Intentional irreversible loss of detail is lossy compression.

definition: The study of the lowest rate needed to represent a source within a chosen average distortion.
wrongs: The study of lossless codes that must stay at or above entropy.
The design of antennas for a radio link.
A test only for prefix-code lengths.
why: It gives the fundamental limit for lossy compression at a specified fidelity.
example: Allowing a larger mean squared error lets a Gaussian source be sent at a lower rate.
scenario: Designers want the minimum bits per sample for a Gaussian source at a stated mean squared error. Which theory sets that limit?
scenarioWhy: The rate-distortion function is the minimum rate for a given distortion.

definition: A dictionary compression method that parses a sequence into phrases without being told the source probabilities.
wrongs: An optimal symbol code that starts from a known probability table.
A block parity code for a binary symmetric channel.
A quantiser with fixed reconstruction levels.
why: It builds a dictionary from the data itself and is universal for a wide class of sources.
example: A compressor stores a repeated sentence by pointing at an earlier matching phrase in the file.
scenario: A compressor discovers repeated phrases in the file and never receives a symbol probability table. Which family is that?
scenarioWhy: Dictionary parsing without prior probabilities is Lempel-Ziv coding.

definition: The set of long sequences whose probability is close to two to the minus n times the entropy.
wrongs: Only the single most probable sequence of length n.
Every possible sequence, each treated as equally important.
The set of codewords at minimum distance.
why: For a large n, almost all the probability sits on this set, which has about two to the nH sequences.
example: For a biased coin, the all-heads string is the most probable but is not typical if heads is rare.
scenario: For a biased coin, the all-heads string is most probable but lies outside the set of sequences we usually see. Which set do the usual sequences form?
scenarioWhy: Sequences with probability near two to the minus nH form the typical set.

definition: For a long memoryless sequence, almost all probability lies on roughly equally likely typical sequences.
wrongs: Every sequence of length n has exactly the same probability.
The most probable sequence contains almost all the probability mass.
Channel noise becomes zero as the block length grows.
why: The law of large numbers makes the sample entropy close to the true entropy for typical sequences.
example: Long tosses of a biased coin almost surely land near the expected fraction of heads, not at all heads.
scenario: As n grows, a memoryless source's probability concentrates on about 2^(nH) similarly likely sequences. Which property says that?
scenarioWrongs: All sequences are exactly equally likely
One sequence holds all the mass
scenarioWhy: Concentration on about 2^(nH) typical sequences is the asymptotic equipartition property.

definition: A channel whose output symbol depends only on the current input, through fixed transition probabilities.
wrongs: A channel that remembers previous inputs and lets them affect later outputs.
A source that emits independent symbols.
A code that maps k bits to n bits.
why: There is no memory: each use is an independent draw from the same input-output distribution.
example: Each bit through a binary symmetric channel is flipped with probability 0.1, independently of other bits.
scenario: Each output depends only on the current input, with the same flip probability every use. Which channel model is that?
scenarioWhy: Independent uses with fixed transitions form a discrete memoryless channel.

definition: The highest mutual information between input and output, which is the top reliable communication rate.
wrongs: The entropy of the source, regardless of the channel.
The bandwidth of the wire measured in hertz only.
The minimum distance of a particular code.
why: Maximising mutual information over input probabilities gives the supremum of rates with vanishing error.
example: A noiseless binary channel has capacity one bit per use because the output can match a full bit of input.
scenario: A noiseless channel takes one binary input and delivers it unchanged. What is its Shannon capacity per use?
scenarioWhy: A perfect binary use conveys one bit, which is the capacity.

definition: Rates below capacity can be made arbitrarily reliable with long codes, while rates above capacity cannot.
wrongs: Noise can be removed by any code, even above capacity.
Reliable communication requires a rate of zero on every noisy channel.
Lossless compression may beat the source entropy.
why: Shannon proved capacity is both achievable in the limit and a hard upper bound.
example: On a channel of capacity 0.5 bit per use, a rate of 0.4 can be reliable, but 0.6 cannot.
scenario: A channel has capacity 0.5 bit per use. Which rate can long codes make arbitrarily reliable?
scenarioWhy: Only rates below capacity are guaranteed to be reliable by the noisy-channel coding theorem.

definition: A binary channel that flips each input bit independently with a fixed crossover probability.
wrongs: A channel that replaces some bits with a known erasure symbol and never flips the others.
A channel that adds Gaussian noise to a continuous amplitude.
A source that emits fair bits.
why: The two possible errors, zero to one and one to zero, are equally likely at the crossover probability.
example: Each transmitted bit is inverted with probability 0.1 and left unchanged otherwise.
scenario: Each bit is flipped independently with probability one half and never erased. What is the channel capacity per use?
scenarioWhy: A binary symmetric channel that flips half the bits conveys no information.

definition: A binary channel that either delivers the input correctly or replaces it with a known erasure.
wrongs: A channel that flips bits without telling the receiver.
A channel that adds continuous Gaussian noise.
A code that repeats each bit three times.
why: The receiver knows which positions were erased, so those positions are lost but not misleading.
example: In each use the bit survives with probability 0.8 and otherwise arrives as an erasure mark.
scenario: A binary erasure channel erases 20 percent of bits and delivers the rest perfectly. What is its capacity per use?
scenarioWhy: Binary erasure capacity is one minus the erasure probability, here 0.8 bit.

definition: Noise that is added to the signal, is Gaussian, and is uncorrelated from sample to sample.
wrongs: Noise that multiplies the signal and arrives only in bursts.
A binary flip process with a crossover probability.
Deterministic interference from one known sinusoid only.
why: Whiteness means a flat spectrum and independent samples; Gaussian noise is fully described by its variance.
example: A baseband receiver sees the sent sample plus an independent normal random variable of fixed variance.
scenario: Each received sample is the sent value plus an independent normal variable of constant variance. Which noise model is that?
scenarioWhy: Independent added Gaussian samples are additive white Gaussian noise.

definition: The capacity of a band-limited Gaussian channel rises with bandwidth and with signal-to-noise ratio.
wrongs: Capacity depends only on the source entropy and not on bandwidth or noise.
A noiseless binary channel always has capacity equal to its bandwidth in hertz.
Widening bandwidth cannot change the reliable bit rate.
why: The theorem gives capacity as bandwidth times the log of one plus the signal-to-noise ratio.
example: Doubling the signal-to-noise ratio of a voice-band modem raises, but does not double, its theoretical rate.
scenario: A designer may widen a Gaussian channel's bandwidth or raise its signal-to-noise ratio. Which theorem says both can raise capacity?
scenarioWhy: Bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio set Gaussian capacity through the Shannon-Hartley theorem.

definition: Adding structured redundancy so a receiver can detect or correct errors introduced by the channel.
wrongs: Removing redundancy so a source uses fewer bits.
Mapping bits to carrier phases.
Choosing a shorter password.
why: The extra structure lets the decoder recognise which codeword was most likely sent.
example: A radio frame adds parity bits so a single flipped bit inside the frame can be corrected.
scenario: Before modulation, a transmitter adds parity so the receiver can repair bit flips. Which task is that?
scenarioWhy: Adding redundancy against channel errors is channel coding.

definition: The fraction of a codeword's symbols that carry information, usually k divided by n.
wrongs: The number of bit errors a code can correct.
The entropy of the message source.
The carrier frequency of the modem.
why: A lower rate means more redundancy and usually more ability to fight noise.
example: A code that maps 4 information bits to 7 transmitted bits has rate 4/7.
scenario: A block code sends 7 bits for every 4 information bits. What is its code rate?
scenarioWhy: Code rate is information symbols over transmitted symbols, so 4/7.

definition: The number of positions in which two equal-length strings differ.
wrongs: The Euclidean gap between two points in a QAM constellation.
The time delay between two multipath echoes.
The difference of two code rates.
why: Each mismatch counts as one, which is the right distance for symbol errors on a discrete channel.
example: The strings 10110 and 10011 differ in two positions, so their Hamming distance is 2.
scenario: Compare 10110 with 10011. What is the Hamming distance?
scenarioWhy: The strings differ in the third and fifth positions, so the distance is 2.

definition: The smallest Hamming distance between any two different codewords of a code.
wrongs: The longest codeword in the code.
The number of information bits k.
The crossover probability of the channel.
why: A larger minimum distance separates codewords so more errors are needed to confuse them.
example: If every pair of codewords differs in at least three positions, the minimum distance is 3.
scenario: A code's closest distinct codewords differ in three positions. How many errors can it correct?
scenarioWhy: A minimum distance of 3 corrects one error, because floor of (3-1)/2 is 1.

definition: An extra bit chosen so the number of ones in a word is even or odd, detecting some errors.
wrongs: A bit that encrypts the payload with a secret key.
A repeated copy of the entire message.
A bit that increases the carrier frequency.
why: A single flip changes the parity, so the check fails, but the bit does not say which position flipped.
example: Even parity turns the data bits 1011 into 10111 because three ones need one more one.
scenario: Even parity is applied to data bits 1011. What parity bit should be appended?
scenarioWhy: Three ones are odd, so the even-parity bit must be 1.

definition: A code that repeats each information bit several times and decodes by majority vote.
wrongs: A code that adds one parity bit to a long data word.
A dictionary compressor for repeated phrases.
A code whose parity bits follow a Hamming parity-check matrix.
why: Repeating a bit n times can correct up to floor of (n-1)/2 errors by choosing the majority value.
example: The bit 1 is sent as 111, and the received word 101 is decoded back to 1.
scenario: Each bit is sent three times and decoded by majority vote. How many bit errors in a triple can this correct?
scenarioWhy: A length-3 repetition code corrects one error and fails if two copies are wrong.

definition: A binary block code that corrects any single error using parity checks on overlapping bit positions.
wrongs: A code that only repeats one bit many times.
A convolutional code with a sliding memory.
A source code built by merging symbol probabilities.
why: The (7,4) Hamming code has minimum distance 3, so one error produces a unique syndrome.
example: Four data bits are encoded into seven bits so that any one flipped bit among the seven can be corrected.
scenario: Four data bits are encoded as seven bits that can correct any single flip. Which code family is that?
scenarioWhy: The binary (7,4) single-error-correcting code is a Hamming code.

definition: Recognising that a received word is not a valid codeword, without necessarily repairing it.
wrongs: Changing the received word back to the unique closest codeword.
Compressing the message before transmission.
Raising transmit power until errors disappear.
why: A failed parity or checksum shows that an error happened even when the correct bits are still unknown.
example: A file checksum does not match, so the transfer is known to be corrupt and is requested again.
scenario: A checksum fails and the receiver asks for a retransmission instead of guessing the data. Which capability was used?
scenarioWhy: Noticing corruption without repairing it is error detection.

definition: Recovering the original codeword from a received word that contains correctable errors.
wrongs: Only noticing that some error occurred and stopping.
Asking the source to use fewer symbols.
Discarding the frame with no attempt to infer the bits.
why: If the number of errors is within the code's correcting power, one codeword is the clear choice.
example: A Hamming decoder sees a nonzero syndrome and flips the single bit that syndrome identifies.
scenario: A decoder uses a syndrome to flip one wrong bit and delivers the original data. Which capability is that?
scenarioWhy: Restoring the transmitted codeword is error correction.

definition: The pattern of parity-check failures that is zero for a codeword and identifies the error otherwise.
wrongs: The information bits before any parity is added.
The entropy of the message source.
The list of all codewords in the codebook.
why: Multiplying by the parity-check matrix yields zero on the code and a fingerprint of a correctable error.
example: A single-error Hamming decoder maps each nonzero syndrome to exactly one bit position to flip.
scenario: The parity checks on a received word all pass, producing an all-zero check result. What does that result say?
scenarioWhy: A zero syndrome means the received word satisfies every parity check.

definition: Further processing of an observation cannot increase the information it carries about the original source.
wrongs: Any function of the output can create extra mutual information about the input.
Compression always raises channel capacity.
Noise can be removed by an arbitrary post-processor with no loss of rate.
why: If the source, the observation, and the processed result form a Markov chain, mutual information cannot rise.
example: Quantising a channel output cannot reveal more about the input than the unquantised output already did.
scenario: A receiver quantises the channel output before decoding. Can that quantised value carry more information about the input than the raw output?
scenarioWrongs: Only if the quantiser is fine
scenarioWhy: The data processing inequality says post-processing cannot create new information about the input.

definition: A bound showing that a small decoding-error probability requires little leftover uncertainty about the input.
wrongs: A rule for building prefix codes from symbol probabilities.
A limit that ignores error probability entirely.
A statement that every noisy channel has capacity zero.
why: If the chance of guessing wrong is small, the conditional entropy of the input given the observation must be small.
example: A decoder that is wrong half the time cannot claim that almost no uncertainty about the message remains.
scenario: A decoder is wrong on half of the blocks. Can the remaining uncertainty about the input be nearly zero?
scenarioWrongs: Only if the code is Huffman
scenarioWhy: Fano's inequality links a large error probability to leftover uncertainty.

definition: A continuous-variable uncertainty measure that can be negative and is not a count of discrete bits.
wrongs: The ordinary entropy of a finite alphabet, which is never negative.
The mutual information of two discrete bits.
The code rate k/n of a block code.
why: It is the integral analogue of entropy; shifting or scaling a density changes it, and small variance can make it negative.
example: A very narrow uniform density on a tiny interval has negative differential entropy.
scenario: A continuous noise variable has a very small variance and its differential entropy is negative. Is that possible?
scenarioWrongs: Only if the variable is constant
scenarioWhy: Differential entropy is not discrete entropy and may be negative.

definition: Mapping a continuous amplitude to one of a finite set of reconstruction levels.
wrongs: Adding parity bits to an already discrete bit string.
Assigning a Huffman code to known symbol probabilities.
Filtering a signal without reducing its amplitude set.
why: Many nearby amplitudes share one level, which introduces quantisation error before digital coding.
example: A microphone sample of 0.37 is stored as the nearest of 256 audio levels.
scenario: An analogue sample is replaced by the nearest of 256 levels before it is coded. Which operation made it discrete?
scenarioWhy: Replacing a continuous amplitude by a finite level is quantisation.

definition: A code whose codeword contains the original information bits unchanged, plus separate parity bits.
wrongs: A code that mixes information so no original bit appears unchanged.
A source code with variable-length words.
A modulation with no extra bits at all.
why: The message can be read directly from the systematic part when the decoder finds no error.
example: A codeword stores four data bits in front and three parity bits after them.
scenario: A codeword begins with the original data bits and appends parity. Which structural property is that?
scenarioWhy: Unchanged information bits plus parity means the code is systematic.

definition: A code that maps each fixed block of k information symbols to a codeword of n symbols.
wrongs: A code that slides continuously over a stream using encoder memory.
A compressor that emits one variable-length word per symbol.
A channel with no coding at all.
why: Successive blocks are encoded separately, as in Hamming and many algebraic codes.
example: Every group of four bits is replaced by a distinct seven-bit word, with no memory of the previous group.
scenario: Each group of k bits is encoded alone into n bits, with no dependence on earlier groups. Which code class is that?
scenarioWhy: Independent mapping of fixed blocks is a block code.

definition: A code that produces parity from a sliding window of recent bits stored in encoder memory.
wrongs: A code that encodes each block with no memory of previous bits.
A prefix source code for single symbols.
A repetition of one isolated bit only.
why: Shift-register memory ties each output to several input bits, and Viterbi decoding searches the resulting trellis.
example: Each new input bit shifts into a register and two parity streams are formed from the bits currently stored.
scenario: Each output depends on the new bit and several previous bits held in a shift register. Which code class is that?
scenarioWhy: Parity from a sliding encoder memory is a convolutional code.

definition: Reordering coded symbols so a burst of channel errors is spread into isolated errors.
wrongs: Sorting source symbols by probability before Huffman coding.
Repeating the same bit in adjacent positions on purpose.
Increasing transmit power during a fade.
why: A code that corrects scattered errors can then handle a burst after the symbols are restored to order.
example: A scratch that ruins twenty adjacent symbols on a link becomes single-symbol errors after deinterleaving.
scenario: A fade corrupts 20 consecutive symbols, but after reordering they fall into separate correctable positions. Which technique did that?
scenarioWhy: Spreading a burst into isolated errors is interleaving.

definition: An unwanted random disturbance added to a signal that can change the received symbol.
wrongs: Structured parity that the encoder adds on purpose.
The information carried by a rare source symbol.
A fixed amplifier gain chosen by the designer.
why: Noise is unpredictable and is not part of the intended signal or the code's deliberate redundancy.
example: Thermal motion of electrons in a receiver adds a small random voltage to every sample.
scenario: A receiver records a random voltage from electron motion even while the transmitter is silent. Which disturbance is that?
scenarioWhy: An unwanted random disturbance at the receiver is noise.
